questions.prompt: An astronaut floats in free space. Which action can change the motion of her centre of mass?
options: Rotating her torso
Shaking her head
Swinging her arms in circles
Throwing an object away from her
questions.explanation: Throwing exchanges momentum with another body; internal motions cannot.

questions.prompt: A quadruped has 12 actuated joints and a free 3D base. How many degrees of underactuation?
questions.explanation: The 6 base coordinates have no actuators.

questions.prompt: A planar biped has 4 joints and a free planar base (3 coordinates). Total generalized coordinates?
Hopper m_b = 3 kg, m_l = 0.5 kg, u = 45 N in stance. Ground force in N (three decimals)?
A hopper with m_b = 3 kg and m_l = 0.5 kg has its foot on the ground and u = 45 N (ground force 49.905 N). COM acceleration in stance in m/s^2 (three decimals, g = 9.81)?
A robot with mu = 0.6 stands on flat ground carrying its full weight. Maximum horizontal COM acceleration in m/s^2 (g = 9.81, three decimals)?

remediationRefs.label: Review: Friction limit on base acceleration

questions.prompt: A hopper's code returns COM acceleration u/(m_b + m_l) - g in flight. What is wrong?
options: The gravity term should be doubled, since both bodies are accelerating
Nothing is wrong, since the actuator force pushes the COM up in flight
The actuator is an internal force and cancels: the result must be -g
The masses should be multiplied, not summed, in the denominator
questions.explanation: Internal action-reaction forces sum to zero.

questions.prompt: A 30 kg robot has a foot support force of 294.3 N acting 0.05 m ahead of its COM horizontally. Torque about the COM in N m (three decimals)?
Body inertia 4 kg m^2, arm 1 kg m^2, zero total angular momentum. The arm rotates 100 degrees relative to the body. Magnitude of the body rotation in degrees?
The first (base) row of M(q) q_ddot + h = S^T tau + J_c^T f contains:
options: only f (and joint accelerations through M_bj), with no tau
tau and f, because the actuators push directly on the base
only tau, because the contact forces act on the joints
neither force nor torque, since it is a pure kinematic relation
questions.explanation: S selects joints, so base rows contain no tau.

questions.prompt: In flight, a robot wants to rotate its body. What can it do?
options: Nothing; orientation cannot change in flight when no external torque acts
Apply a torque from the air by pushing against it with the feet
Move limbs to rotate the body while angular momentum stays constant
Change its COM trajectory with joint torques to reorient the body
questions.explanation: Internal motion can reorient the body; momentum constraints remain.

questions.prompt: A controller commands a humanoid a horizontal COM acceleration of 8 m/s^2 on a floor with mu = 0.5. Predict what happens and why.

remediationRefs.label: Review: Friction limit on base acceleration

rubric: Computes the limit mu g = 4.9 m/s^2 for full weight support.
Concludes feet slip because required friction exceeds the cone.
Suggests reducing the command, increasing normal force, or using other contacts.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the hopper, how the same actuator force gives different centre-of-mass accelerations in flight and in stance.
rubric: Flight: internal forces cancel, COM acceleration -g.
Stance: ground force f = u + m_l g enters the COM equation.
Concludes contact is the channel by which actuators influence the base.

questions.prompt: A robot on flat ground with mu = 0.4 must accelerate its centre of mass forward at 4 m/s^2. What is the minimum upward centre-of-mass acceleration z'' (m/s^2) for which the friction bound |x''| <= mu (z'' + g) allows it? Use g = 9.81.

remediationRefs.label: Review: Friction bound with vertical acceleration

questions.explanation: From |x''| <= mu(z'' + g): 4 <= 0.4 (z'' + 9.81), so z'' >= 4/0.4 - 9.81 = 10 - 9.81 = 0.19 m/s^2. At constant height the bound is mu g = 3.924 < 4, so the push is impossible; the robot must press into the ground slightly harder than its weight.

questions.prompt: A 30 kg robot has its centre of mass 0.9 m above flat ground and accelerates with x'' = 2 m/s^2 and z'' = 1.5 m/s^2 with zero angular acceleration. Using (m z'' + m g)(x_cp - x) = (z_cp - z) m x'' - I theta'', find the horizontal offset x_cp - x (in m) of the centre of pressure from the centre of mass. Use g = 9.81.
questions.skillLabel: Centre of pressure from moment balance

remediationRefs.label: Review: Centre of pressure from moment balance

questions.explanation: With theta'' = 0 and z_cp = 0: (30 * 1.5 + 30 * 9.81)(x_cp - x) = (0 - 0.9) * 30 * 2, i.e. 339.3 (x_cp - x) = -54. Hence x_cp - x = -54/339.3 = -0.159 m: the CoP is 0.159 m behind the centre of mass. A common error is to use the ZMP shortcut with z'' = 0, which gives -0.1835 and ignores the extra vertical force.

questions.prompt: A standing robot (mu = 0.6, centre of mass 0.9 m high, foot reaching 0.25 m behind the centre of mass) accelerates forward at constant height. Its maximum acceleration is limited by the centre-of-pressure condition (2.725 m/s^2), not by friction (5.886 m/s^2). Which change raises the maximum forward acceleration?
options: Fit higher-friction soles (increase mu)
Use motors with a higher torque limit
Lengthen the foot behind the centre of mass
Make the robot heavier
questions.explanation: At constant height the ZMP relation gives x''_max = g * l_b / z, with l_b the reach of the foot behind the centre of mass; lengthening the heel side raises it. More friction does not help because friction is not the binding constraint (5.886 > 2.725). Motor torque does not enter the base rows of the dynamics, and mass cancels in x'' = g (x - x_cp)/z.
